newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, out of hospital, faces host of problems.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, out of hospital, faces host of problems.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin spends his first full day out of hospital for almost two weeks on Tuesday, facing deep economic and political problems in Russia and the prospect of tough negotiations with NATO.

The 65-year-old president left Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital on Monday after 12 days of treatment for double pneumonia and travelled to the Gorky-9 state residence just outside Moscow to complete his convalescence.
"There is no point in expecting the president to rush back to full-time work, which also means the Kremlin," presidential press secretary Sergei Yasztrzhembsky said.

Despite this, Yeltsin will be chomping at the bit to prove wrong the political foes who say he is not well enough to rule the vast country of 150 million people after suffering pneumonia just two months after heart surgery.

In foreign policy, he faces tough negotiations in the next few months over NATO's plans to expand eastwards after alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov failed to break the impasse at talks on Monday.
"The meeting was useful although, of course, there are different approaches on a range of questions," the foreign ministry said in a statement.
"Discussions will be continued. A timetable has been set for future work. It is clear that it will not be easy but the two sides will try to make them a success."
Solana and Primakov met for five hours outside Moscow and declined to talk to reporters -- an indication of the sensitivity of the talks and how much importance the two sides attach to the outcome.

NATO officials and diplomats in Brussels said the very fact that negotiations had started represented a step forward -- even though they said both sides simply used the occasion to underline how far apart they were.

NATO is expected to issue membership invitations at a summit next July to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Moscow says such moves threaten its security and that it is considering measures to respond to NATO enlargement.
At home, Yeltsin faces deep economic problems headed by widespread discontent over unpaid wages to millions of workers.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin could address this problem in Yeltsin's absence on Tuesday when he meets about 30 newly-elected members of the Federation Council, the upper house of parliament.

Other problems include a lack of progress in army reforms, constant attacks from opponents who want Yeltsin removed on health grounds and the danger of tension mounting as separatist leaders in Chechnya continue to say their region is independent.

Fighting with Russian forces over Chechnya's independence demands ended after 21 months last August, but all the candidates in Chechen elections scheduled for January 27 insist on independence even though Moscow has ruled it out.
A peace accord last August deferred solving the question of Chechnya's status for five years.

"Whoever comes to power in Chechnya, in any situation, Chechnya will conduct itself as an absolutely independent state," General Lev Rokhlin, head of the Russian lower house of parliament's defence committee, told NTV commercial television.

"the contradiction is the main thing. Russia will not agree to sovereignty for Chechnya and Chechnya will do all it can to confirm its sovereignty," said Rohklin, who fought in Chechnya before he took up politics.
